title: Class balance per age group
what_it_shows: The number of records in each class (No ASD traits, ASD traits) for the four age groups after cleaning.
how_to_read_it: Each age group has two bars. A taller bar means more records in that class.
main_finding: The groups are unbalanced in different directions. Toddlers are mostly positive and adults are mostly negative.
example: Toddlers: 690 positive and 283 negative (71% positive). Adults: 185 positive and 506 negative (27% positive).
where_it_is_used: Slides (EDA). Earlier draft of the paper.

title: Age distribution by class
what_it_shows: How old the people are in each age group, coloured by class.
how_to_read_it: The x-axis is age (months for toddlers, years for the others). The height of a bar is the number of people. The two colours are stacked on top of each other.
main_finding: Age does not separate the two classes in a clear way.
example: In the toddler panel both colours appear at every age from 12 to 36 months.

title: Questionnaire score by class
what_it_shows: The total score (sum of the ten answers, 0 to 10) in each age group, coloured by class. The dashed line is the cut-off.
how_to_read_it: Look at the dashed line. Everything on the right of it is one colour (ASD traits) and everything on the left is the other colour.
main_finding: The two classes never overlap. The label is exactly: score above the cut-off. This is the key finding of the project.
example: For adults the cut-off is 6. Every adult with a score of 7 or more is labelled ASD traits, and every adult with 6 or less is not.
where_it_is_used: Slides (Understanding the data). Earlier draft of the paper.

title: Share of answers scored 1, by age group and class
what_it_shows: For each question (A1 to A10), the share of people who scored 1, shown for each age group and each class.
how_to_read_it: Each cell is a number from 0 to 1. A darker cell means more people scored 1 on that question. Compare the 'ASD' column with the 'No' column of the same age group.
main_finding: Some questions separate the classes strongly and others are scored 1 by both classes.
example: Illustration: a cell of 0.90 in an 'ASD' column next to 0.20 in the 'No' column means that question separates the two classes well.

title: Chi-square statistic of each input against the label
what_it_shows: How strongly each input (ten questions, sex, jaundice, family history) is related to the label, for each age group.
how_to_read_it: Chi-square is a number that measures a relation. A bigger number (darker cell) means a stronger relation with the label.
main_finding: The questions are strongly related to the label. The personal details are only weakly related.
example: Illustration: an input with a value of 300 is much more strongly related to the label than an input with a value near 1.
where_it_is_used: Slides (EDA). The same ranking is used in notebook 08 to pick the 4, 6 or 8 most useful questions.

title: Correlation between questions A1 to A10
what_it_shows: How much each pair of answers goes together, for each age group.
how_to_read_it: Correlation goes from -1 to 1. Red means two answers tend to be 1 together. Blue means when one is 1 the other tends to be 0. White means no relation.
main_finding: No two questions always go together. The correlations between different questions lie between -0.16 and 0.54 across the four age groups.
example: The diagonal is always dark red, because every question is perfectly related to itself (correlation 1).

title: ROC-AUC across the 15 test folds
what_it_shows: The spread of ROC-AUC over the 15 test folds for each model, one panel for each age group.
how_to_read_it: ROC-AUC shows how well a model ranks people (1.0 is perfect, 0.5 is guessing). A narrow box means stable results. A wide box means the result changes a lot between folds.
main_finding: For toddlers, children and adults, LR, EBM and TabPFN are a single line at 1.0. For adolescents every model spreads widely.
example: A box from 0.95 to 1.00 for adolescents means the model scored 0.95 in some folds and 1.00 in others.
where_it_is_used: Slides (Spread across folds and sanity checks).

title: Recall across the 15 test folds
what_it_shows: The spread of recall over the 15 test folds for each model, one panel for each age group.
how_to_read_it: Recall is the share of real positive cases that the model finds. Example: 9 found out of 10 is 0.9. Read the boxes as in the ROC-AUC figure.
main_finding: The tree models (RF, XGB, LGBM) miss more positive cases than LR, EBM and TabPFN.
example: For adults, Random Forest has a mean recall of 0.941, so it misses about 6 positive cases in 100. EBM has 1.000.
where_it_is_used: Notebook 06. Numbers are in the paper (Table III).

title: Calibration of the six models
what_it_shows: Whether the percentages given by each model can be trusted, one panel for each age group.
how_to_read_it: The x-axis is what the model says (predicted probability). The y-axis is what is true (share really positive). A model on the dashed diagonal line is well calibrated.
main_finding: EBM lies on the diagonal for toddlers, children and adults. Logistic Regression is far from it in the middle. For adolescents all models jump, because few predictions fall in the middle.
example: If a model says 80% for a group of people and 80% of them are really positive, its point lies on the dashed line.
where_it_is_used: Supporting material (Fig. S1). Numbers are in the paper (Table IV).

title: Nemenyi post-hoc p-values for ROC-AUC
what_it_shows: For each pair of models, the p-value of the Nemenyi test, one panel for each age group.
how_to_read_it: A p-value below 0.05 (red) suggests the two models differ. Green means no clear difference.
main_finding: LR, EBM and TabPFN do not differ from each other. This figure is only a description, because the folds are not independent.
example: Illustration: a red cell of 0.01 between two models suggests they differ. A green cell of 0.90 means no difference was found.

title: Cross-source ROC-AUC (train on one source, test on another)
what_it_shows: ROC-AUC of each model when it is trained on one dataset and tested on a dataset from a different source.
how_to_read_it: There are four groups of bars: two toddler pairs on the left and two adult pairs on the right. Each colour is one model.
main_finding: Toddler bars are all close to 1.0, which is expected because both datasets use the same rule. The UCI to Kaggle adult bars drop to about 0.87 to 0.90.
example: Trained on UCI adults and tested on Kaggle adults, EBM scores 0.879. On its own data it scored 1.000.
where_it_is_used: Slides (Cross-source test). Numbers are in the paper (Table V).

title: Reduced questionnaire: ROC-AUC against the number of questions
what_it_shows: ROC-AUC of each model when it only gets 4, 6, 8 or all 10 questions.
how_to_read_it: The x-axis is the number of questions available. Each line is one model. A line that falls to the left means the model gets worse with fewer questions.
main_finding: No model is perfect with fewer questions. All models fall at a similar rate.
example: For children, EBM scores 1.000 with 10 questions, 0.980 with 8, 0.945 with 6 and 0.886 with 4.

title: Noisy answers: ROC-AUC against the share of answers flipped
what_it_shows: ROC-AUC of each model when 0%, 5%, 10% or 20% of the test answers are flipped at random.
how_to_read_it: The x-axis is the share of answers that were changed (a 0 becomes 1 or a 1 becomes 0). Each line is one model. Lines fall to the right.
main_finding: All models lose accuracy at about the same rate. 5% noise costs about 0.02 and 20% noise costs about 0.10 to 0.17.
example: For adults, EBM scores 1.000 with no noise, 0.985 with 5%, 0.962 with 10% and 0.897 with 20%.

title: Feature importance by explanation method
what_it_shows: The importance that EBM, SHAP and LIME give to each input, averaged over 10 splits. Each column is scaled to add up to 1.
how_to_read_it: Each row is an input and each column is a method. A cell of 0.10 means that input carries one tenth of the total importance under that method.
main_finding: Each of the ten questions gets about 0.10. Age, sex, jaundice and family history get almost nothing.
example: For adults under LIME every question is between 0.098 and 0.101, so LIME sees them as almost equal.

title: SHAP values of the EBM on the test set
what_it_shows: The SHAP value of each input for every person in the test set of the first split, one panel for each age group.
how_to_read_it: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) shares a prediction out between the inputs. Each dot is one person. Red dots are answers scored 1. Dots on the right push the prediction towards ASD traits, dots on the left push it away.
main_finding: For every question, answers scored 1 (red) push the prediction up and answers scored 0 (blue) push it down, as the scoring rule implies.
example: A red dot far to the right on the A5 row is a person whose answer to question 5 raised the model's score a lot.

title: Result page of the web tool
what_it_shows: The result page of the web tool for an example toddler screening.
how_to_read_it: The top part shows the questionnaire score and the cut-off. This is the main result. Below it is the model output, with a note that it is not the chance that the person has autism.
main_finding: The tool shows the standard score first and the model second, as the supervisor asked.
example: The example toddler has a score of 7 out of 10. The cut-off is above 3, so the answers show signs of autistic traits. The model output is 100%.
